result: The study characterized the kinematics of self-generated head movements in freely moving rats (n=16), finding that head rotations occurred more frequently along pitch and yaw axes than roll, with angular speeds of 18-287°/s and frequencies up to 20 Hz. Gravitational acceleration dominated low-frequency (<2 Hz) components of acceleration signals, while non-gravitational acceleration arose primarily from head rotations.
evaluation: Claims C32-C41 provide comprehensive quantitative characterization of head movement kinematics with appropriate sample size (n=16 rats), statistical measures, and frequency analysis. The data are internally consistent and supported by multiple supplementary figures showing power spectra, autocorrelation, and component separation.

result: A total of 86 units were recorded and classified into putative Purkinje cells (90%), Golgi cells (5%), and mossy fibers (5%) using established criteria. Putative Purkinje cells exhibited irregular inter-spike intervals at rest with an average CV of 0.95 ± 0.58.
evaluation: Claims C42-C44 describe the recorded neural population with clear sample sizes and classification criteria based on established methods (Van Dijck et al., 2013). The CV measurement is quantitative and appropriate for characterizing firing irregularity. The classification is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3E.

result: Using a model-free resampling approach, the study found that firing rate predictability was greatest when considering angular velocity combined with either acceleration or gravitational acceleration (mean R²=0.17±0.13, n=86 units). Gravitational information dominated the effect of acceleration on firing rate (p<8e-9), suggesting cerebellar units preferentially exhibited mixed sensitivity to head rotations and head tilt.
evaluation: Claims C45-C49 present the core methodological finding with appropriate statistical comparisons and validation. The model-free approach was validated by showing high correlation between independent estimates (R=0.65±0.23) versus shuffled controls (R=0.14±0.10, p=2.2×10⁻¹⁶). The conclusion about mixed sensitivity is well-supported by the comparative R² values.

result: Neighboring units displayed positive correlations in their instantaneous firing rates (R=0.14±0.26, n=35 pairs, p=0.0014) that were lost with time-reversal controls. Correlations were higher when comparing firing rate estimates (R=0.31±0.47, p=0.0013) than instantaneous rates, indicating neighboring units shared similar sensitivities to head movements.
evaluation: Claims C50-C53 and C88 demonstrate spatial organization of cerebellar responses with appropriate controls (time-reversal) and statistical tests. The finding that correlations are stronger for movement-related components than raw firing rates supports the interpretation of shared receptive fields in microzones.

result: The presence or absence of light did not change the correlation between independent firing rate estimates (p=0.87, n=23), showing limited influence of visual cues on units' sensitivity to head movements.
evaluation: Claims C54, C55, and C77 provide a clear experimental manipulation (light vs. dark) with appropriate statistical testing showing no significant effect. The sample size (n=23) is adequate for this comparison, and the result is consistent across claims.

result: Firing rate estimates from passive sessions significantly differed from estimates obtained using observations from the active session (p=0.0021, n=17), suggesting that units' coding schemes differed when movements were self-generated versus passively experienced.
evaluation: Claims C56-C57 show a significant difference between active and passive conditions, but C85 and the passive movement characterization (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) reveal that passive movements had different kinematic properties (lower frequencies, smaller range of head orientations). The observed differences could reflect incomplete sampling of the parameter space rather than fundamental differences in coding, making the interpretation uncertain.

result: A fraction (20%) of caudal cerebellar units displayed selective tuning to either head angular velocity (Ω-units, n=6) or head tilt (AG-units, n=12). Ω-units exhibited higher rotational gain (0.28±0.15 °⁻¹) than AG-units (0.03±0.02 °⁻¹, p=0.0012) and mixed units (0.07±0.05 °⁻¹, p=0.00022), with preferred rotation axes clustered around semi-circular canal directions. Most putative granular layer units (6/8) belonged to these selective categories.
evaluation: Claims C58-C64, C68-C69 characterize selective units with clear classification criteria (eightfold difference in R²), quantitative comparisons of gain, and anatomical validation. The finding that granular layer units are predominantly selective is consistent with their role as input pathways. Sample sizes are small but appropriate for this subpopulation analysis.

result: AG-units were strongly modulated by head tilt with simple receptive fields, while Ω-units were not modulated by head tilt (CV of firing rate: 2.28 vs. 0.29, p=0.0047). AG-units were classified as putative mossy fibers (n=1), Golgi cells (n=3), and Purkinje cells (n=8).
evaluation: Claims C65-C67 provide clear quantitative differentiation between AG-units and Ω-units using CV of firing rate across head tilts, with appropriate statistical testing. The cell type classification is consistent with the overall population distribution.

result: The rotational sensitivity of most units with mixed sensitivity was highly tilt-dependent. The stability index was lower for non-Ω-units (σx=0.36±0.32, σy=0.41±0.29, n=60) than for Ω-units (σx=0.73±0.13, σy=0.88±0.06, n=6; p=0.0027 and p=0.00011), confirming that the rotational tuning of the largest fraction of the cell population was head tilt-dependent.
evaluation: Claims C70-C72 and C89 demonstrate tilt-dependent rotational tuning using a quantitative stability index with appropriate statistical comparisons. The finding is supported by visual examples in Figure 4A-F and applies to the majority of the recorded population (60/86 units).

result: A subpopulation of Purkinje cells (n=7 external-coding, n=5 internal-coding) exhibited tuning to rotations about axes defined in either earth-bound or head-bound reference frames, isolated using a collinearity cutoff (difference >0.5 or <-0.5 for angular distances 80-100°). External-coding cells' preferred rotation axes did not cluster around specific directions.
evaluation: Claims C73-C75, C8, and C82 describe a novel finding of reference frame-specific coding with clear quantitative criteria for classification. The analysis method (collinearity as a function of angular distance) is appropriate for detecting reference frame alignment. The sample sizes are small but the effect is clear in individual examples (Figure 5C-F).

result: The rotational sensitivity of units was maximal for positive lags relative to angular velocity, suggesting it was driven by sensory cues rather than motor commands.
evaluation: Claim C76 is supported by the temporal lag analysis showing positive optimal lags (0.5±21.8 ms for Ω-units, 29.8±142.4 ms for mixed units), consistent with sensory-driven responses. This interpretation is reasonable given the known delays in sensory processing.

result: Global linear models always produced poorer predictions than the model-free approach (p=1e-13), while local linear models (tilt-dependent rotational sensitivity) performed equivalently to the model-free approach (p=0.24, n=86 units), indicating that the nonlinearity in firing rate responses is mainly due to head tilt-dependence of linear rotational sensitivity.
evaluation: Claims C78-C80 provide a critical comparison of modeling approaches with appropriate statistical testing. The finding that local linear models match the model-free approach while global models fail supports the interpretation that tilt-dependent linear tuning captures the essential nonlinearity. This is demonstrated across multiple model variants in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

result: The caudal cerebellar vermis hosts a re-encoded, gravitationally polarized representation of self-generated head kinematics in freely moving rats, where most Purkinje cells exhibited mixed sensitivity to head rotational and gravitational information and were differentially modulated by active and passive movements.
evaluation: Claims C6, C7, C9, C81, and C100 represent the main conclusions of the study, supported by the comprehensive experimental findings including: (1) mixed sensitivity demonstrated by model-free analysis (C45-C48), (2) tilt-dependent rotational tuning (C70-C72), (3) reference frame-specific coding in a subpopulation (C73-C75), and (4) equivalence of local linear models to model-free approach (C78-C80). The convergent evidence from multiple analytical approaches strongly supports this conclusion.

result: Gravitationally polarized rotational sensitivity requires complex re-encoding of head-centered sensory cues and might subserve downstream computations such as encoding head direction in the earth-horizontal plane. Purkinje cells encoding rotations relative to gravity could subtract the component of rotations that changes head orientation relative to gravity from semi-circular canal inputs.
evaluation: Claims C83-C84 and C91-C92 are speculative interpretations about functional roles and computational mechanisms. While C90 is a logical inference about coordinate transformations, the proposed mechanisms for how these signals might be used downstream lack direct experimental support. These are reasonable hypotheses but require additional experiments to validate.

result: The instantaneous firing rate of many units exhibited strong fluctuations even during complete immobility and was only loosely connected to the rapid component of head inertial signals, consistent with coding of information at the level of Purkinje cell populations.
evaluation: Claims C86-C87 describe an important observation about firing rate variability (CV=0.95±0.58 from C44) and its interpretation. The interpretation is supported by citation to Herzfeld et al., 2015 and by the finding that neighboring cells show correlated movement-related components (C50-C53), consistent with population coding.

result: The study proposes circuit mechanisms for generating gravitationally polarized receptive fields, involving unipolar brush cells smoothing otolithic signals, granule cells as coincidence detectors, and climbing fiber teaching signals from inferior olive neurons influenced by both external afferents and Purkinje cell feedback.
evaluation: Claims C93-C99 propose detailed circuit mechanisms based on anatomical knowledge and cited literature, but lack direct experimental validation in this study. While the proposed mechanisms are plausible and well-grounded in cerebellar circuitry, they remain speculative hypotheses requiring targeted experiments to test.

result: The introduction establishes the scientific context: head movements are sensed in head-bound coordinates but must be transformed to earth-centered coordinates for self-orientation, requiring integration of vestibular signals (from semi-circular canals and otolith organs) with gravity information. The caudal cerebellar vermis is implicated in this transformation based on lesion studies and prior recordings in passive conditions.
evaluation: Claims C1-C31 provide background knowledge supported by appropriate citations. The logical progression from the computational problem (C1-C3) through the relevant anatomy and physiology (C10-C31) to the knowledge gap (C4, C27) effectively motivates the study. All claims are either established knowledge or supported by cited literature.

result: The transformation of head-bound peripheral vestibular signals into earth-bound representations involves complex nonlinear computations whose detailed mechanisms remain to be elucidated. The caudal cerebellar cortex is in a key anatomical position immediately downstream of vestibular organs and upstream of vestibular nuclei.
evaluation: Claims C101-C103 accurately summarize the state of knowledge and identify remaining questions. C101 is supported by citation to Green and Angelaki, 2007, C102 acknowledges the knowledge gap, and C103 states established anatomical relationships that motivate studying this region.

result: The study used sixteen adult male Long-Evans rats (aged 3-4 months, 250-300g at surgery) with all procedures approved by the Charles Darwin Ethics Committee (project number 1334) and conducted in compliance with French national and European laws.
evaluation: Claims C104-C106 provide standard methodological information about experimental subjects and ethical compliance. The information is clear and complete.
